## Getting started with a template

There are a few different types of reports available:

* **empty**: A blank report template that includes the VISC header, but no other text.
* **generic**: A PT report template that includes generic text that can be adapted to your statistical analysis.
* **bama**: A PT report template for the BAMA assay.
* **nab**: A PT report template for the NAb assay.

To use a VISC report template, run:

```{r eval=FALSE}
use_visc_report(
  report_name = "VDCnnn_BAMA_PTreport_interim_blinded", # the name of the report file
  path = "BAMA", # the path within the active directory, usually the name of the assay
  report_type = "bama" # "empty", "generic", "bama", or "nab"
)
```

If you choose any `report_type` other than `"empty"`, this will set 
up a specific structure in the directory specified in `path`. Continuing with the BAMA
example above, this structure looks like:

```
|- BAMA/
|  +- VDCnnn_BAMA_PTreport_interim_blinded/              
|     +- VDCnnn_BAMA_PTreport_interim_blinded.Rmd       # VISC report template
|     +- methods/                                       # folder with "child" .Rmd documents
|       +- biological-endpoints.Rmd
|       +- lab-methods.Rmd
|       +- statistical-methods.Rmd
```

The "child" R Markdown documents contain standardized language for the methods
sections of PT reports. 
Edit these as needed for the specifics of your analysis.

You can use a VISC report template through the RStudio GUI 
(`File > New File > Rmarkdown... > From Template`), 
or with `rmarkdown::draft()`,
but this does not automatically generate the "child" R Markdown documents, 
so you will have to do that manually or with `use_visc_methods()` if you choose this option.

## Knit to PDF or Word

The VISC report R Markdown template knits to either a PDF or Word document. 

* Use the Knit button select either the PDF (visc_pdf_document) or 
Word (visc_word_document) output.
* Note the shortcut Ctrl-Shift-K will run the first output in the YAML, will be the last output run (starts off as PDF first).
* If you want to run both reports in one command, either use `rmarkdown::render()` with `output_format = 'all'`, or install the loom package and create a RStudio Addin (<https://github.com/thebioengineer/loom>).


## Using the template 

There are some new functions and coding conventions that help with knitting the report to both outputs.

### Page breaks

* For page breaks use `insert_break()` function.
    
### Referencing
`
**Figure and table references**

* For figure and table references use `insert_ref()` function.
    + For example: `` `r knitr::inline_expr("insert_ref('fig:response-rate-plot')")` ``.
* Make sure chunk names only use dashes or referring will not work (no spaces or underscores).
* Do not use figure or table labels in chunk headings or kable code (e.g., don't use `fig.cap = "My Figure Caption \\label{my_figure_label}"`. Rmarkdown will automatically assign the chunk name as the figure/table reference label.

**Sections** 

* For referencing sections, use `insert_ref()` but you must list both the section label and the desired section name
    + For example: `` `r knitr::inline_expr("insert_ref('referencing', 'Referencing')")` `` gives `r VISCtemplates::insert_ref('referencing', 'Referencing')`.
    + For example: `` `r knitr::inline_expr("insert_ref('page-breaks', 'Page breaks')")` `` gives `r VISCtemplates::insert_ref('page-breaks', 'Page breaks')`.
* For PDF output the matching section number is display regardless of the section name listed.
* For Word output the section name listed is displayed.

**References/Bibliography**

*  For referencing papers inline, simply use the @ symbol before bib file reference (e.g., "As specified in `@Huang:2013fl`, ...").
*  For referencing papers in parentheses at the end of a sentence, use brackets and the @ symbol (e.g., `[@Huang:2013fl]`). The parentheses will be automatically included - do not add any extra.
*  For multiple papers in the same citation, separate with a semicolon (e.g., ` [@Suissa1985; @Lyderson2009]`). The parentheses will be automatically included - do not add any extra.

### Tables

* For tables written directly in an R Markdown chunk, output only one table per chunk.
  To generate many tables in a loop, use `insert_tab_subchunk()` as shown below;
  it gives each table its own generated chunk.
* `insert_tab_subchunk()` accepts both `knitr::kable()` and
  `flextable::flextable()` tables. Set captions and formatting on the table
  object before inserting it.
* For `kable()` tables, use `format = output_type`, where the report template
  defines `output_type` as `"latex"` for PDF or `"pandoc"` for Word.
  Word cannot support many kableExtra features, such as
  `kableExtra::kable_styling()`. Use `warning = kable_warnings` on chunks
  using those features to avoid unwanted warnings in Word output.
* Table labels use the chunk name prefixed with `"tab:"`. For example,
  `tab_chunk_name = "descriptive-stats"` gives `"tab:descriptive-stats"`,
  which can be passed to `insert_ref()`. Generated chunk names must be
  unique throughout the document; use hyphens rather than spaces or underscores.
* For table-specific settings, see the
  [kable reference](https://pkg.yihui.org/knitr/manual#kable) and
  [R Markdown Cookbook's kable guide](https://pkg.yihui.org/rmarkdown-cookbook/kable),
  or the flextable guide to
  [rendering and chunk options](https://ardata-fr.github.io/flextable-book/rendering.html)
  and [captions](https://ardata-fr.github.io/flextable-book/captions-and-cross-references.html).

The examples below are intended for a VISC PDF/Word report with
`library(VISCtemplates)` loaded. They are not evaluated in this HTML vignette.
Use `results = 'asis'` on the calling chunk so the generated output is
interpreted as document content, and `echo = FALSE` to hide the calling code.

#### A kable table

Set the full caption with `caption` and, for the PDF List of Tables, a short
caption with `caption.short`.

```{r kable-example, eval=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  head(mtcars),
  format = output_type,
  caption = "Motor car data. The first six observations are shown.",
  caption.short = "Motor car data"
)
```

#### A flextable

Set the full caption with `flextable::set_caption()`. Apply
`ft_add_short_caption()` after all other flextable formatting to add a short
caption for the PDF List of Tables; Word output is unchanged. Supply
LaTeX-ready text for `short`, escaping special characters as needed
(e.g., `"Response (50\\%)"`). If `short` is omitted, the helper derives
a short caption from the full caption using a sentence-boundary heuristic;
provide it explicitly when the caption contains abbreviations.

```{r flextable-example, eval=FALSE, results='asis'}
ft <- flextable::flextable(head(mtcars))
ft <- flextable::autofit(ft)
ft <- flextable::set_caption(
  ft, caption = "Motor car data. The first six observations are shown."
)
ft <- ft_add_short_caption(ft, short = "Motor car data")
ft
```

### Figures

* For figures written directly in an R Markdown chunk, output only one figure
  per chunk. To generate figures in a loop, use `insert_fig_subchunk()`;
  it gives each figure its own generated chunk, caption, and reference label.
* Figure labels use the chunk name prefixed with `"fig:"`. For example,
  `fig_chunk_name = "my-boxplot"` gives `"fig:my-boxplot"`, which can be
  passed to `insert_ref()`. Use unique chunk names with hyphens rather than
  spaces or underscores.
  
### Many tables/figures in a loop

This example generates one figure and one table per cylinder group in a
single loop. Each figure and table gets a unique chunk name, allowing
captions and references to be assigned separately.

Use `results = 'asis'` so the generated output is interpreted as document
content, and `echo = FALSE` to hide the calling code. This example assumes
`library(VISCtemplates)` is loaded.

```{r tables-figures-loop, eval=FALSE, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
car_groups <- split(mtcars, mtcars$cyl)

for (group in names(car_groups)) {
  group_data <- car_groups[[group]]
  group_label <- paste("Cars with", group, "cylinders")

  # Insert one figure for this group.
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(group_data, ggplot2::aes(wt, mpg)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point()

  insert_fig_subchunk(
    fig = p,
    fig_chunk_name = paste0("weight-vs-mpg-", group),
    fig_caption_short = paste("Fuel efficiency:", group, "cylinders"),
    fig_caption_long = paste(
      "Car weight versus fuel efficiency for cars with", group, "cylinders."
    ),
    fig_height = 4,
    fig_width = 6
  )

  # Insert one table for this group.
  ft <- flextable::flextable(group_data)
  ft <- flextable::autofit(ft)
  ft <- flextable::set_caption(
    ft,
    caption = paste0(group_label, ". All observations are shown.")
  )
  ft <- ft_add_short_caption(ft, short = group_label)

  insert_tab_subchunk(
    ft,
    tab_chunk_name = paste0("car-data-", group)
  )
}
```

To use a `kable()` table instead, replace the flextable creation and
insertion code inside the loop with:

```{r loop-kable-alternative, eval=FALSE}
tab <- knitr::kable(
  group_data,
  format = output_type,
  caption = paste0(group_label, ". All observations are shown."),
  caption.short = group_label
)
insert_tab_subchunk(tab, tab_chunk_name = paste0("car-data-", group))
```

`insert_fig_subchunk()` accepts ggplot objects and other supported printable
graphics, not base R plotting calls. The optional `fig_height` and
`fig_width` arguments specify dimensions in inches during knitting; omit
them to use inherited knitr dimensions.

When run interactively, the subchunk helpers print the object directly
instead of generating a chunk. Knit the report to check captions,
reference labels, and figure dimensions.

### P values

* When using `VISCfunctions::pretty_pvalues()` make sure to use `output_type = output_type`,  `bold  = pandoc_markup`, and `italic = pandoc_markup`. This will give the appropriate markup depending on PDF or Word output.

### Sourcing external R scripts

* When using the `source()` function for external R scripts, use its `local = TRUE` argument. This will ensure that the objects created are placed in your Rmd's environment, rather than your global environment, which is a safer practice.

### Loading external data

* When using the `data()` function to load external data (e.g. from another package), specify `environment = environment()`. This will ensure that the object is placed in your Rmd's environment, rather than your global environment, which is a safer practice. See the "Good practice" section in `?utils::data` for more info.
